title: Ace Declarations
summary: When an Ace hits the pile, the player declares a new suit. Build the declaration popup with Godot Control nodes, an enum-backed OptionButton, and a signal that carries the choice back to the rules engine.

lessons.title: A Suit-Declaration Popup
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Control Nodes and the Declaration Popup

A **Control** node is Godot's base class for UI — buttons, labels, dialogs. When a player plays an Ace they must declare the next suit; that is a perfect fit for a popup built from Control nodes.

```gdscript
class_name DeclareSuitDialog
extends Control

signal suit_declared(suit: int)

@onready var option_button: OptionButton = $Panel/OptionButton
@onready var confirm_button: Button = $Panel/ConfirmButton

func _ready() -> void:
    option_button.add_item("Hearts", CardTypes.Suits.HEARTS)
    option_button.add_item("Diamonds", CardTypes.Suits.DIAMONDS)
    option_button.add_item("Clubs", CardTypes.Suits.CLUBS)
    option_button.add_item("Spades", CardTypes.Suits.SPADES)
    confirm_button.pressed.connect(_on_confirm)

func _on_confirm() -> void:
    var suit: int = option_button.get_selected_id()
    suit_declared.emit(suit)
    hide()
```

`@onready` resolves the node reference after the scene is ready, safer than `$Panel/OptionButton` at the top of the script (the child might not exist yet). `OptionButton.add_item(label, id)` lets us store the enum value as the item's id, so `get_selected_id()` returns the enum directly — no string parsing, no lookup table.

The dialog emits `suit_declared` and hides itself. The rules engine connects to `suit_declared` and updates the required suit. The dialog has no idea what the rules do with the answer — pure decoupling.

> [!WHY]
> Storing the enum value as the OptionButton id means a rename of the suit string never breaks the rules. If we had string-matched on `"Hearts"`, a typo or localisation would silently break the game. The enum-as-id pattern keeps UI text and rule logic independent — translate the labels freely; the selected id is always a valid `Suits` member.

Hide dialogs rather than `queue_free()`-ing them if you will reuse them; recreating nodes each turn is wasteful.

practicePrompt.instructions: Add a Cancel button that emits nothing but hides the dialog. Wire it up in _ready() and write the handler.
practicePrompt.hint: Use a second @onready var and connect its pressed signal.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why use `@onready` instead of initialising the node reference at the top of the script?
choices: Children may not exist when the script loads; @onready defers resolution until _ready() runs after the tree is built
quizQuestions.explanation: Node paths resolve only after the scene tree is constructed. @onready guarantees the reference is fetched at the right moment.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the advantage of storing the enum value as the OptionButton item id?
choices: `get_selected_id()` returns the enum directly, so UI text can be translated without affecting rule logic
quizQuestions.explanation: Decoupling the displayed label from the underlying value means localisation and rule logic never interfere — the id is always a valid Suits member.

lessons.title: Enforcing the Declared Suit
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Enforcing the Declared Suit

The popup from the last lesson collects the player's choice — but a declaration means nothing until the rules engine **enforces** it. When an Ace is played and a suit declared, the next player must play that suit; the ordinary match-suit-or-rank rule is suspended until the demand is met.

We model this with one extra piece of game state: `declared_suit`. A sentinel value of `-1` means "no declaration active", so the variable doubles as its own on/off switch.

```gdscript
var declared_suit: int = -1  # -1 = no active declaration

func _on_suit_declared(suit: int) -> void:
    declared_suit = suit

func is_playable(card: CardData, top: CardData) -> bool:
    if declared_suit != -1:
        return card.suit == declared_suit or card.rank == CardTypes.Ranks.ACE
    return card.suit == top.suit or card.rank == top.rank

func on_card_played(card: CardData) -> void:
    if declared_suit != -1 and card.suit == declared_suit:
        declared_suit = -1  # demand satisfied — clear it
```

`is_playable` now has two modes. While a declaration is active, only the declared suit (or another Ace, which lets a player re-declare) gets through; the top card's suit and rank are irrelevant. Once no declaration is active, the familiar Phase 0 rule takes over.

The third function is the easy one to forget: **clearing** the declaration. The moment a card of the declared suit lands, the demand is satisfied and `declared_suit` returns to `-1`. Skip this step and the declaration haunts every later turn, locking the whole game to one suit forever.

> [!WHY]
> Temporary rule modifiers like a suit declaration have a full **lifecycle**: set, enforce, clear. Bugs cluster at the edges — a declaration that is never cleared, or one cleared too early (before any matching card was played). Writing the three lifecycle functions side by side, and naming the sentinel (`-1`) explicitly, makes each stage visible and testable. Any future modifier — an active penalty, a pending question — follows the same set/enforce/clear shape.

Connect the dialog's `suit_declared` signal to `_on_suit_declared` and the loop is closed: UI collects the choice, state stores it, `is_playable` enforces it, and the first conforming card clears it.

codeSnippets.caption: The declaration lifecycle: store on Ace, enforce in is_playable, clear when satisfied.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write `has_declaration()` returning true while a declaration is active, and `describe_demand()` returning e.g. "Play Hearts" using a SUIT_NAMES dictionary, or "No demand" when inactive.
practicePrompt.hint: Compare declared_suit against the -1 sentinel; use SUIT_NAMES[declared_suit] for the label.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does `declared_suit` use -1 as its inactive value instead of a separate `has_declaration: bool` flag?
choices: A sentinel keeps the state in ONE variable, so it can never disagree with a companion flag — two variables can drift out of sync
quizQuestions.explanation: With a value-plus-flag pair, a bug can set the flag without the value (or vice versa). A single sentinel-bearing variable makes the invalid combination unrepresentable.

quizQuestions.prompt: What goes wrong if `on_card_played` never resets `declared_suit` to -1?
choices: The declaration stays active forever, so every future turn is locked to that one suit and the game effectively jams
quizQuestions.explanation: State modifiers must be cleared when satisfied. A stale declaration keeps overriding is_playable on every later turn — the classic 'forgot the clear step' lifecycle bug.
